title.en: What a network is, and why we layer it
title.zh: 网络是什么，为什么要分层

description.en: Work out how one computer gets a message into another's hands: the Internet versus the World Wide Web, the ways of classifying networks by transmission method, scale and shape, and why we layer, encapsulate, and tell services from protocols.
description.zh: 弄清两台电脑怎样把一条消息送到对方手里：互联网与万维网的区别，网络按传输方式、规模、形状的分法，以及为什么要分层、封装、区分服务与协议。

name.en: Internet architecture; the Internet vs. the WWW
name.zh: 互联网的结构，以及互联网与万维网的区别 (Internet architecture; Internet vs. WWW)
客户端-服务器模型 (client-server model)
传输技术：广播与点对点 (broadcast vs. point-to-point)
按规模分类的网络 (networks by scale)

name.en: Network topologies: mesh, bus, star, ring
name.zh: 网络拓扑：网状、总线、星型、环型 (mesh, bus, star, ring)

name.en: Protocol layering: layers, protocols, interfaces, services
name.zh: 协议分层：层、协议、接口、服务 (layers, protocols, interfaces, services)
封装与解封装 (encapsulation and decapsulation)
面向连接与无连接服务 (connection-oriented vs. connectionless)
服务与协议的关系 (relationship of services and protocols)

description.en: Thinking the Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing; in fact the Web is just one application running on the Internet.
description.zh: 以为互联网和万维网是同一个东西；其实万维网只是跑在互联网上的一种应用。

description.en: Thinking a client and a server are two kinds of machine; in fact they are roles played by processes, and one machine can play both at once.
description.zh: 以为客户端和服务器是两种机器；其实它们是进程扮演的角色，一台机器可以同时扮演两种。

description.en: Treating a “broadcast network” (how the wire is shared) and “broadcast” (sending to everyone) as the same thing, or thinking every machine that receives a packet on a broadcast network will process it.
description.zh: 把『广播网络』（线怎么共用）和『广播』（发给所有人）当成一回事，或以为广播网络里收到分组的机器都会处理它。

description.en: Mixing up protocol and interface: a protocol is horizontal, an agreement between the same layer on two hosts; an interface is vertical, the boundary between two adjacent layers on one host.
description.zh: 分不清协议和接口：协议是横向的、两台主机同一层之间的约定；接口是竖向的、同一台主机相邻两层之间的边界。

description.en: Treating a service and a protocol as the same thing; a service says what is done, a protocol says how it is done.
description.zh: 把服务和协议当成一回事；服务说『做什么』，协议说『怎么做』。

description.en: Thinking connection-oriented always means reliable and connectionless always means bad; the two simply make different trade-offs between reliability and overhead.
description.zh: 以为面向连接就一定可靠、无连接就一定不好；两者只是在可靠性和开销之间做不同的取舍。

title.en: The smallest network

prompt.en: In your dorm you open www.unimelb.edu.au. The other end of your laptop's cable is a network with many machines, and your message has to reach the one called the server. Besides the wire, what does this message need at the very least?
prompt.zh: 你在宿舍点开 www.unimelb.edu.au。笔记本的线另一头连着一个有很多台机器的网络，你的消息要到那台叫服务器的机器手里。除了线，这条消息至少还需要什么？

label.en: Nothing; the wire carries it to the right machine by itself
label.zh: 什么都不用，线会自己把它送到对的机器

feedback.en: A wire only carries the signal; it does not know who is who. With many machines, the message has to say where it is going.
feedback.zh: 线只管把信号带过去，它不认识谁是谁。机器一多，消息就得自己说清要去哪里。

label.en: An address saying who it is for
label.zh: 一个标明『送给谁』的地址

label.en: A computer faster than the server
label.zh: 一台比服务器更快的电脑

feedback.en: Speed only affects how fast it arrives, not who it goes to.
feedback.zh: 速度只影响送得多快，不影响送给谁。

explain.en: To find the server among many machines, the message must carry the other side's address, which is what the IP address is for. Next we start from the smallest network and lay these words out one by one.
explain.zh: 在很多台机器里找到服务器，消息上得写着对方的地址，这就是 IP 地址的用处。下面从最小的网络开始，把这些词一个个摆出来。

title.en: One computer, one wire, one server
title.zh: 一台电脑，一条线，一台服务器

text.en: Shrink everything to the minimum first. On the left is your laptop, on the right is the school's server, with one wire in between. You press Enter, and the laptop sends out a message that travels along the wire to the server.

alt.zh: 左边是笔记本（客户端），右边是服务器，中间一条线，线上有一个写着目标地址和来源地址的分组

caption.zh: 图中的 IP 地址只是示意

text.en: The figure already holds the first few words of this lesson:
text.zh: 图里已经有了这一课的头几个词：

items.en: **Network device**: a machine attached to the network. Laptops, phones, routers and switches all count.
items.zh: **网络设备** (network device)：接在网络上的机器。笔记本、手机、路由器、交换机都算。

items.en: **Client**: the side that takes the initiative and asks for a service; here, your laptop.
items.zh: **客户端** (client)：主动上门、请求服务的一方，这里是你的笔记本。

items.en: **Server**: the side that waits there, accepts requests and provides the service; here, the school's website machine.
items.zh: **服务器** (server)：等在那里、接受请求并提供服务的一方，这里是学校的网站机器。

items.en: **Packet**: one message sent between two devices, like a parcel with the address written on it.
items.zh: **分组** (packet)：两台设备之间发出的一条消息，像一个贴好地址的包裹。

items.en: **IP address**: a unique number that identifies a device, like the recipient and sender addresses on a parcel.
items.zh: **IP 地址** (IP address)：标识一台设备的唯一数字，相当于包裹上的收件地址和寄件地址。

text.en: A pile of devices joined by wires, able to pass things among themselves, is a **network**: many similar parts joined together, able to pass information between the parts.
text.zh: 一堆设备靠线连起来，能在彼此之间传东西，就是**网络** (network)：许多相似的部分互连，能在部分之间传递信息。

text.en: The slides put it more narrowly for a **computer network**: a set of **autonomous** computers joined by a **single technology**. “Autonomous” means each machine can run on its own, and is not someone else's dumb terminal; “single technology” means the same kind of wire and the same way of signalling joins them. Keep this wording in mind. Once we have seen what the Internet looks like, we will come back and ask: does the Internet count?
text.zh: 课件对**计算机网络** (computer network) 的说法更窄：一组**自治** (autonomous) 的计算机，用**单一技术**互连。『自治』是说每台机器自己能独立运转，不是别人的哑终端；『单一技术』是说连它们的是同一种线、同一种信号方式。这个说法先记着。等看完互联网的样子，我们会回头问：互联网算不算？

title.en: Question and answer: the ones really talking are processes
title.zh: 一问一答：真正说话的是进程

text.en: A server does not send you things for no reason. When you open a web page, you ask first and it answers: one **request**, one **reply**. This division of labour, question and answer, is called the **client-server model**.
text.zh: 服务器不会无缘无故给你发东西。你点开网页，是你这边先问，它那边才答：一条**请求** (request)，一条**回复** (reply)。这种一问一答的分工，叫**客户端-服务器模型** (client-server model)。

alt.en: The client process in the client machine sends a request across the network to the server process in the server machine; the server process sends the reply back
alt.zh: 客户端机器里的客户进程发出请求，穿过网络到服务器机器里的服务进程；服务进程把回复送回来

caption.en: The request and the reply go back and forth between two processes across the network
caption.zh: 请求和回复穿过网络，在两个进程之间往返

text.en: Look closer: the ones talking are not the machines but the programs running in them, that is, **processes**. The browser on your laptop is the client process; the website software on the school's machine is the server process.
text.zh: 细看一下，说话的并不是机器，而是机器里跑着的程序，也就是**进程** (process)。你笔记本上的浏览器是客户进程，学校机器上的网站软件是服务进程。

text.en: So “client” and “server” name **roles**, not kinds of machine. One machine can run a client process and a server process at the same time. When a piece of website software asks a database for data, it is a client of the database.
text.zh: 所以『客户』和『服务器』说的是**角色**，不是机器的种类。同一台机器可以同时跑着客户进程和服务进程。一个网站软件向数据库要数据的时候，它对数据库来说就是客户。

text.en: Why divide the work this way? Because a server has to face many clients at once. It waits at a fixed address and answers whoever asks; clients can come and go, and the server does not need to know in advance who will come. Slide 9 draws two clients connected to the same server, which is what this means.
text.zh: 为什么这样分工？因为服务器要同时面对很多客户。它守在一个固定的地址上等着，谁来问就答谁；客户可以来来去去，服务器不用提前知道谁会来。课件第 9 页画了两个客户端连着同一台服务器，就是这个意思。

title.en: One laptop, two roles

prompt.en: You run a small website program on your laptop to debug an assignment, and a classmate's browser visits this site on your laptop over the dorm network. At the same time, your own browser is visiting the school's website. Which statement about your laptop is true?
prompt.zh: 你在笔记本上开了一个小网站程序，用来调试作业；同学的浏览器通过宿舍网络访问你笔记本上的这个网站。同时，你自己的浏览器也在访问学校的网站。关于你的笔记本，哪句话对？

label.en: It is a server in both cases, because it is a computer
label.zh: 它在这两件事里都是服务器，因为它是一台电脑

feedback.en: A computer has no identity as “client” or “server” by itself; it is the processes running on it that play the roles.
feedback.zh: 电脑本身没有『客户』或『服务器』的身份，是跑在上面的进程在扮演角色。

label.en: In the first case it runs a server process, in the second a client process, so it plays both roles at once
label.zh: 它在第一件事里跑着服务进程，在第二件事里跑着客户进程，同时扮演两种角色

label.en: A machine can only pick one role, so the two cannot happen at the same time
label.zh: 一台机器只能选一个角色，所以这两件事不可能同时发生

feedback.en: The role belongs to the process. One machine can have many processes at once, each playing its own part.
feedback.zh: 角色属于进程。一台机器上可以同时有很多进程，各演各的。

label.en: It is a client, because it is not server hardware bought for the purpose
label.zh: 它是客户端，因为它不是专门买来的服务器硬件

feedback.en: Assigning roles by how good the hardware is is a common misunderstanding. As long as it waits for others to ask and answers them, it is acting as the serving side.
feedback.zh: 按硬件好坏分角色是常见的误解。只要它在等别人来问、并回答，它就在当服务方。

explain.en: Client and server are roles that processes play in one communication: whoever speaks first with a request is the client; whoever waits and replies is the serving side. One machine can have both kinds of process at once.
explain.zh: 客户端和服务器是进程在一次通信里扮演的角色：谁先开口请求，谁就是客户；谁守着等待并回复，谁就是服务方。同一台机器可以同时有两种进程。

title.en: The Internet and the Web

prompt.en: In everyday talk people mix up “going online”, “going on the Internet” and “going on the Web”. Do you think the Internet and the World Wide Web (WWW) are the same thing?
prompt.zh: 日常里大家把『上网』『上互联网』『上万维网』混着说。你觉得互联网 (the Internet) 和万维网 (WWW) 是同一个东西吗？

label.en: The same thing, just two names
label.zh: 是同一个东西，只是两个名字

feedback.en: In daily use they are mixed up, but technically they are not the same.
feedback.zh: 日常里确实混着用，但技术上不是一回事。

label.en: No: the Internet is the whole network underneath, and the Web is one application running on top of it
label.zh: 不是：互联网是下面的一整张网，万维网是跑在它上面的一种应用

label.en: No: the Web is the thickest backbone lines inside the Internet
label.zh: 不是：万维网是互联网里最粗的那几条骨干线路

feedback.en: The Web is not a line. It is a system made of web pages, browsers and servers; the lines belong to the Internet.
feedback.zh: 万维网不是线路。它是靠网页、浏览器和服务器组成的一套系统，线路属于互联网。

explain.en: The answer is b. First look at what the Internet itself looks like, then come back and explain the Web properly.
explain.zh: 答案是 b。先看互联网自己长什么样，再回来把万维网说清楚。

title.en: Follow a packet across the Internet
title.zh: 顺着一个包，走过互联网

text.en: The architecture diagram on slide 4 draws a lot of things at once. Ignore the labels for now and follow the thick line: your request leaves home and goes all the way to a server in a machine room.

alt.zh: 一个请求从家出发，经接入网、ISP 的接入点 POP、本地 ISP 骨干，通过互联进入另一家 ISP 骨干，最后到达数据中心或内容分发网络

caption.en: Follow the thick line on slide 4
caption.zh: 沿课件第 4 页那条粗线走一遍

rows.en: Access network (fibre FTTX, DSL, cable)
rows.zh: 接入网 (光纤 FTTX、DSL、有线电视)

rows.en: The last stretch from home to the ISP. DSL borrows the telephone line, and the DSLAM at the other end gathers many homes' lines together; cable borrows the TV line, with a cable modem at home and a CMTS at the other end collecting the homes
rows.zh: 家到 ISP 的最后一段。DSL 借电话线，对面的 DSLAM 把许多家的线汇在一起；有线电视借电视线，家里用 cable modem，对面的 CMTS 汇集各家

rows.en: A single router cannot join a home to its ISP; a dedicated line has to run to the neighbourhood or the machine room
rows.zh: 家和 ISP 之间不能只靠一台路由器，得有一条专门的线通到小区或机房

rows.en: Point of presence (POP)
The ISP's local “doorway”, where many homes' lines converge and enter the ISP's own network
rows.zh: ISP 在本地设的『门口』，许多家庭的线在这里汇聚，进入 ISP 自己的网络

rows.en: An ISP cannot run a direct line from every home to its machine room; gathering traffic locally first is cheapest
rows.zh: ISP 不可能给每户都拉一条直通机房的线，先在本地汇聚最省

rows.en: Backbone
A network the ISP builds from routers, with thick lines that run far
rows.zh: ISP 内部用路由器连成的网，线路粗、跑得远

rows.en: Traffic from many places has to be moved around, which takes thick, fast trunk lines
rows.zh: 要把很多地方的流量搬来搬去，需要粗而快的干线

rows.en: Peering
Two ISPs join their networks at certain places and hand over each other's traffic
rows.zh: 两家 ISP 在某些地方把网络接起来，互相转交对方的流量

rows.en: An ISP only connects its own users; without peering, your ISP could not reach other people's servers
rows.zh: 一家 ISP 只连着自己的用户；不互联，你的 ISP 就够不着别人的服务器

rows.en: Data centres, CDNs
A data centre is a machine room full of servers; a content delivery network (CDN) keeps copies of popular content closer to users
rows.zh: 数据中心是放着大量服务器的机房；内容分发网络 (CDN) 把热门内容的副本放在离用户更近的地方

rows.en: Fetching the same popular video from a distant machine room every time would fill the long-distance lines, and you would wait longer
rows.zh: 每次都从远处的机房取同一部热门视频，长途线路会被占满，你也要等得更久

text.en: “Why must ISPs peer with each other?” is the question this figure most wants you to think through. The Internet is not one company's network, but many independently run networks joined together. If they connect, any two machines can talk; if they do not, you get a set of islands.
text.zh: 『为什么 ISP 之间一定要互联』是这张图最该想明白的一问。互联网不是某一家公司的网，而是许多各自独立运营的网络接在一起。接得上，任意两台机器才通；接不上，就是一个个孤岛。

title.en: Three questions along this road

body.en: Every stretch of the road makes you ask the same three things: how much can it carry (bandwidth), how long does it take (delay), and does anyone peek or tamper on the way (security). Bandwidth and delay are in lessons 3 and 4; security is in lessons 17 to 19.
body.zh: 沿路每一段都会让你问同样三件事：能带多少 (带宽)，多久能到 (延迟)，中途有没有人偷看或改动 (安全)。带宽和延迟在第 3、4 课，安全在第 17 至 19 课。

title.en: The Internet is a network of networks; the Web is just one application
title.zh: 互联网是网络的网络，万维网只是其中一个应用

text.en: Back to the question left hanging. Slide 2 says a computer network is “autonomous computers joined by a single technology”, and slide 6 says the Internet is a “network of networks”. Does the Internet count as a computer network?
text.zh: 回到那个悬着的问题。课件第 2 页说计算机网络是『用单一技术互连的自治计算机』，第 6 页又说互联网是『网络的网络』。互联网算不算计算机网络？

text.en: Look at the road we just walked: at home it is Wi-Fi plus fibre, inside the ISP it is another kind of line, and inside the data centre it is another set again. **Each small piece** uses one consistent technology inside, so it is a computer network in the sense of slide 2. The Internet joins these many pieces together, so it is not “one network of one technology” but a **network of networks**.
text.zh: 看刚才的路：家里是 Wi-Fi 加光纤，ISP 内部是另一种线路，数据中心里又是另一套。**每一小块**内部用着统一的技术，是第 2 页意义上的计算机网络。互联网是把这许多块再接起来，所以它不是『一种技术的一张网』，而是**网络的网络** (network of networks)。

title.en: How to answer in the exam

body.en: The answer on slide 6: the Internet is not a single network but a network of networks.
body.zh: 课件第 6 页的答案：互联网不是单个网络，而是网络的网络。

text.en: The Web is a different idea
text.zh: 万维网是另一层意思

text.en: The **World Wide Web (WWW)** is a **distributed system** made of many **web pages**, the Web servers that store them, and the **browsers** you use to view them: pages are scattered over servers around the world and tied together by links. It **runs on top of the Internet**.
text.zh: **万维网** (World Wide Web, WWW) 是由很多**网页**、存放网页的 Web 服务器、以及你用来看网页的**浏览器**组成的**分布式系统** (distributed system)：页面分散在世界各地的服务器上，靠链接串起来。它**跑在互联网之上** (runs on top of the Internet)。

text.en: What does “on top of” mean? The Internet only takes care of delivering packets to the right machine. What the software on that machine does with them after delivery is another matter. The Internet is like a country's road network, and the Web is one kind of service on it; email, video calls and online games are other fleets of vehicles driving on the same roads.
text.zh: 『在……之上』是什么意思？互联网只负责把分组送到对的机器。送到之后，那台机器里的软件怎么用它，是另一回事。互联网像全国的公路网，万维网像其中一种服务；电子邮件、视频通话、联机游戏是别的车队，走的是同样的路。

text.en: The things slide 5 lists, resource sharing (printers, files), looking things up, entertainment, e-commerce, social networking, and the Internet of Things (parking, smart meters, vending machines), are all applications on the Internet. The Web is just the most famous of them.
text.zh: 课件第 5 页列的资源共享（打印机、文件）、查资料、娱乐、电商、社交，以及物联网（停车、智能电表、售货机），都是互联网上的应用。万维网只是其中最出名的一个。

title.en: Beyond the slides

body.en: Why do the two statements look contradictory? Because “network” means different things at different sizes: inside one small network there is a single technology, while the Internet as a whole joins those pieces together. Once you separate the two, the two sentences on the slides fit together.
body.zh: 为什么两处说法看着冲突？因为『网络』在不同大小上说的是不同的东西：一小块网络内部是单一技术，整个互联网则是把这些块连起来。把这一点分清，课件的两句话就接上了。

title.en: Can your roommate's phone hear it?

prompt.en: You and your roommate are both on the dorm Wi-Fi. Your laptop sends a packet addressed to the router. Your roommate's phone is right next to you. Can its wireless card “hear” this packet?
prompt.zh: 你和室友都连着宿舍的 Wi-Fi。你的笔记本发出一个分组，目标是路由器。室友的手机就在旁边。它的无线网卡能『听到』这个分组吗？

label.en: No: everyone has a private wire to the router
label.zh: 听不到：每个人和路由器之间都有一条专属的线路

feedback.en: Wireless signals spread in all directions; there are no private wires.
feedback.zh: 无线信号是向四周散开的，没有专线。

label.en: Everyone can receive the signal, but it is not addressed to the phone, so the card glances at the address and drops it
label.zh: 信号人人都收得到，只是不是发给它的，网卡看一眼地址就丢掉

label.en: It can receive it, and the phone reads the content and hands it to an app
label.zh: 收得到，而且手机会把内容读出来交给应用

feedback.en: A packet not addressed to you is simply dropped by the network card and never passed up.
feedback.zh: 不是发给自己的分组，网卡会直接丢掉，不会交给上层。

explain.en: The dorm's wireless channel is a stretch of “air” that everyone shares. The signal spreads in all directions and anyone can receive it, and the destination address in the packet decides whether to take notice. This is a broadcast-style network.
explain.zh: 宿舍的无线信道是大家共用的一片『空气』，信号向四周散开，谁都收得到，靠分组里的目标地址决定要不要理会。这就是广播式的网络。

text.en: Classified by **how the signal travels**, there are two big kinds of network.
text.zh: 按**信号怎么传**来分，网络有两大类。

caption.en: One shared wire, or links in pairs
caption.zh: 共用一条线，还是一对一对地连

items.en: **Broadcast network**: all machines share one communication channel. Like shouting in a classroom, the whole class hears it. Each machine that receives a packet glances at the destination address: if it names itself, it processes the content; if not, it acts as if it heard nothing.
items.zh: **广播网络** (broadcast network)：所有机器共用一条通信信道。像在教室里喊一嗓子，全班都听得见。每台机器收到分组，看一眼目标地址：是叫自己，就处理内容；不是，就当没听见。

items.en: **Point-to-point network**: made of connections between pairs of machines. Like passing notes, a note goes only through the people it needs to, and nobody else sees it.
items.zh: **点对点网络** (point-to-point network)：由许多对机器之间的连接组成。像传纸条，一张纸条只经过需要经过的人，别人看不到。

text.en: A broadcast network uses the **address** to tell “is this for me?”. This is also why every packet has to carry a destination address at the front.
text.zh: 广播网络靠**地址**分辨『这是不是给我的』。这也是为什么每个分组前面都要带着目标地址。

text.en: One more meaning: how many people it is sent to
text.zh: 再看一层意思：发给几个人

rows.en: Unicast
One
Calling out Xiao Ming by name
Multicast
Some of the machines in the network
“Students who chose this course, attention please”
Broadcast
All machines in the network
“Everyone in the class, attention please”

title.en: Two meanings of “broadcast”

body.en: “Broadcast network” is about how the wire is shared; “broadcast” as a way of sending is about who it is sent to. They are two different ideas. In a broadcast network you can still unicast: the wire is shared by everyone, but this message names only one person, and everybody else hears it, looks at the address, and drops it.
body.zh: 『广播网络』说的是线怎么共用；『广播』这种发送方式说的是发给谁。两者是两层意思。在广播网络里照样可以单播：线是大家共用的，但这条消息只点了一个人的名，其余的人听到后看地址、丢掉。

title.en: What is the basis of the classification?

prompt.en: Bluetooth earbuds, dorm Wi-Fi, a campus network, a city network, a cross-continent network: people sort networks into these classes. What do you guess the classification mainly looks at?
prompt.zh: 蓝牙耳机、宿舍 Wi-Fi、校园网、一座城市的网络、跨洲的网络：人们把网络分成这几类。你猜，分类最主要看什么？

label.en: Transmission speed
label.zh: 传输速度

feedback.en: Speeds within one class can differ a lot, and a LAN can be much faster than a WAN, so speed is not the basis of the classification.
feedback.zh: 同一类网络的速度可以差很多，一个局域网可以比广域网快得多，所以速度不是分类的依据。

label.en: The distance between machines
label.zh: 机器之间的距离

label.en: Which brand the devices are
label.zh: 设备是哪个品牌

feedback.en: Brand has nothing to do with the size of a network.
feedback.zh: 品牌和网络大小没有关系。

label.en: How many machines are in the network
label.zh: 网络里有多少台机器

caption.en: PAN personal area network, LAN local area network, MAN metropolitan area network, WAN wide area network
caption.zh: PAN 个人区域网，LAN 局域网，MAN 城域网，WAN 广域网

text.en: The table in the slides has only one axis: how far apart the machines are. From the 1 m personal area network (PAN), to local area networks (LAN) of a room, a building and a campus, to the metropolitan area network (MAN) of a city, to the wide area networks (WAN) of a country or continent, and finally the Internet covering the whole globe.
text.zh: 课件的表格只有一根轴：机器之间隔多远。从 1 米的个人区域网 (PAN)，到房间、楼、校园的局域网 (LAN)，到城市的城域网 (MAN)，到国家、洲的广域网 (WAN)，最后是覆盖全球的互联网。

text.en: Why does distance matter so much? Because when it changes, three things change with it:
text.zh: 为什么距离这么重要？因为它一变，三件事跟着变：

items.en: **Delay**: the farther the signal goes, the later it arrives. In one classroom you hardly notice; across a continent it is tens of milliseconds at least (lesson 3 will calculate it).
items.zh: **延迟**：信号走得越远，到得越晚。同一间教室里几乎感觉不到，跨洲就是几十毫秒起（第 3 课会算）。

items.en: **Cost**: the longer the wire, the more it costs. In a room you just run a wire yourself; across a city you have to dig trenches and lay fibre.
items.zh: **成本**：线越长越贵。屋里自己拉一根线就行，跨城市要挖沟、铺光缆。

items.en: **Who owns it**: PANs and LANs usually belong to a person or an organisation, who manages them; MANs and WANs are mostly built by telecom operators and rented by others.
items.zh: **谁拥有**：个人区域网和局域网通常归一个人或一个机构，自己管；城域网、广域网大多靠电信运营商建设，别人租来用。

title.en: The boundaries are man-made

body.en: There is no physical cliff between 10 m and 100 m. PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN are just names that make talking easier. For a large campus network, some people would say LAN and others MAN, and both are defensible. In the exam, answer by the table in the slides.
body.zh: 10 米和 100 米之间没有任何物理上的断崖。PAN、LAN、MAN、WAN 只是方便交流的叫法。一个大型校园网，说它是 LAN 还是 MAN 都有人说得通。考试按课件的表来答。

caption.en: Four ways to connect the same five devices
caption.zh: 同样五台设备的四种连法

text.en: Full mesh: count the wires first
text.zh: 全网状：先数线

text.en: **Full mesh**: every device has its own dedicated point-to-point wire to every other device. With 5 computers, each connects to the other 4, giving 5×4 = 20 wire ends; each wire has two ends, so there are 10 wires. In general, $n$ devices need $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ wires. 100 devices is 4950 wires: the wire count grows with the square of the number of devices, so once there are many devices it becomes too expensive to lay.
text.zh: **全网状** (fully mesh)：每台设备和其他所有设备之间各有一条专用的点对点线。5 台电脑，每台连其他 4 台，一共 5×4 = 20 个线头；每条线有两个头，所以是 10 条线。一般地，$n$ 台设备要 $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ 条线。100 台就是 4950 条：线数随设备数的平方往上涨，设备一多就铺不起。

rows.en: Full mesh
Every machine has a dedicated wire to every other machine
rows.zh: 每台和所有其他台各有一条专线

rows.en: Wire count n(n−1)/2; too expensive to lay once there are many devices
rows.zh: 线数 n(n−1)/2，设备一多就铺不起

rows.en: Each pair has a wire to itself, so no contention; if one wire breaks, the rest carry on as usual
rows.zh: 每对设备独享一条线，不用争；一条线断了，别的照常通

rows.en: Bus
All devices attach to the same shared wire
rows.zh: 所有设备接在同一条共享的线上

rows.en: Only one can send at a time; two sending together collide, so there must be a way to negotiate
rows.zh: 同一时刻只能一台发，两台同时发就冲突，必须有协商办法

rows.en: The least wire; adding a device just means plugging it in
rows.zh: 线最省，加一台设备只要接上去

rows.en: Star
All devices connect to one central device
rows.zh: 所有设备接到一个中心设备

rows.en: If the centre fails everything is cut off; the centre must take many wires
rows.zh: 中心坏了全部断开；中心要接很多条线

rows.en: One broken wire affects only one machine; easy to add devices and easy to find faults
rows.zh: 一条线坏了只影响一台，容易加设备、容易查故障

rows.en: Ring
Each machine takes in the previous machine's data and passes it to the next
rows.zh: 每台收下前一台的数据，再转给下一台

rows.en: One failure breaks the ring; when several want to send, access control decides whose turn it is, e.g. token ring
rows.zh: 一台坏了环就断；多台想发时要有访问控制来决定轮到谁，例如令牌环 (token ring)

rows.en: Little wire; each segment is just a point-to-point link; rules queue the senders, so there are no collisions
rows.zh: 线不多，每一段只是一对点对点，靠规则排队，没有冲突

title.en: The vague line about rings

body.en: The slides say a ring needs “access control to resolve propagation queuing”, which is a bit vague. Think of it this way: data travels around the ring one stop at a time, and when several devices want to send there must be rules to queue them and decide who goes first. Token ring does it by passing around a “token”, and only the holder may send.
body.zh: 课件说环型要『访问控制来解决 propagation queuing』，这个说法有点含糊。可以这样想：数据在环上一站一站传，多台设备都想发时，得有规则排队、决定谁先。令牌环的办法是传一个『令牌』，拿到令牌的才能发。

title.en: Beyond the slides

body.en: Today's Ethernet is almost all switched. The hub marked at the centre of the star diagram in the slides copies whatever it receives out of all the other ports unchanged, so logically it is still one shared wire. A switch, on the other hand, knows who is behind each port and forwards the packet only to the one destination port. Buses and hubs are used here mainly to explain the idea of “sharing one wire”; in the exam, answer by the topology definitions in the slides. Lesson 7 covers this in detail.
body.zh: 今天的以太网几乎都是交换式的。课件星型图里中心标的 hub，会把收到的东西原样从其他所有口转出去，所以逻辑上仍然是一条共享的线。交换机 (switch) 则认得每个口后面是谁，只把分组转给目标那一个口。总线和 hub 在这里主要用来讲清『共用一条线』这个想法；考试按课件的拓扑定义答。第 7 课会细讲。

title.en: How many wires to join every pair

prompt.en: In a dorm building, 20 computers are to be joined directly in pairs (full mesh). How many wires have to be laid in all?
prompt.zh: 宿舍楼里 20 台电脑要两两直接相连（全网状）。一共要拉多少条线？

hints.en: How many other machines does each one connect to?
How many times is each wire counted when you count “how many others each one connects to”?
hints.zh: 每条线被『每台连其他几台』数了几次？

explain.en: Each connects to the other 19, so 20×19 = 380 wire ends; each wire has two ends, so 380 ÷ 2 = 190 wires. The same 20 machines in a star need only 20 wires, at the price that everything is cut off if the centre fails: this is the trade-off behind “why pick this one”.
explain.zh: 每台连其他 19 台，20×19 = 380 个线头；每条线有两个头，380 ÷ 2 = 190 条。同样 20 台连成星型，只要 20 条线，代价是中心设备坏了全断：这就是『为什么选这种』要权衡的东西。

title.en: The philosophers, the translators and the secretaries

text.en: For one computer to get a message into another's hands, there is actually a pile of things to do: recognise the other side, cut the message into suitable pieces, turn it into signals, send it down the wire... One program doing all of it would be hard to write and hard to change. The answer is **layering**: each layer does only one thing and hands the rest to the layer below.
text.zh: 两台电脑要把一条消息送到对方手里，要做的事其实一大堆：认出对方、切成合适的块、变成信号、送过线……一个程序全包，写不动，也改不动。办法是**分层** (layering)：每一层只做一件事，剩下的交给下一层。

text.en: Slide 17 uses a story. A philosopher in place A wants to say “I like rabbits” to a philosopher in place B, but they share no language and are not in the same place.
text.zh: 课件第 17 页用了一个故事。A 地的哲学家想对 B 地的哲学家说『I like rabbits』，可他们没有共同语言，也不在同一个地方。

alt.en: Sites A and B each have three layers: philosopher, translator and secretary. At A the message passes down layer by layer, travels over the fax line to B, then passes up layer by layer; dashed lines between the same layers show a “conversation”
alt.zh: A、B 两地各有哲学家、翻译、秘书三层；A 地信息一层层往下传，经传真线送到 B 地，再一层层往上交；同一层之间用虚线表示『对话』

caption.en: Solid lines are the path the message really takes; dashed lines are each layer's idea that it is talking to its peer
caption.zh: 实线是信息真正走的路，虚线是各层以为自己在对话

text.en: See two things clearly. **First**, a translator “talks” only with the translator on the other side, in a format the two have agreed on (Dutch text plus a language tag); the philosopher need not care, and neither need the secretary. **Second**, the path the message really takes is: the philosopher hands it to the translator, the translator hands it to the secretary, the fax line carries it across, and on the other side it is handed up layer by layer. Each layer uses only the service of the layer **immediately below** it.
text.zh: 看清两件事。**第一**，翻译只和对面的翻译『说话』，用的是两边约好的格式（荷兰语文加一个语言标签）；哲学家不用管，秘书也不用管。**第二**，信息真正走的路是：哲学家交给翻译，翻译交给秘书，传真线送过去，对面再一层层往上交。每一层只用它**下面紧邻**那一层的服务。

text.en: The benefits of this arrangement are real. Replace the secretary (fax becomes email) and the translator and philosopher need not know a thing; if the translators want a different intermediate language, they only need to switch to the same one on both sides, and the secretary sends as before. Each layer can be designed and upgraded independently.
text.zh: 这样安排的好处很实在。换掉秘书（传真改成邮件），翻译和哲学家一点都不用知道；翻译想换一种中转语言，只要两边的翻译换成一样的，秘书照样发。每一层可以独立设计、独立升级。

title.en: What to take from this analogy

body.en: There is no need to force the translator onto some specific layer. Two things are what to understand: a layer talks only with the same layer on the other side; and layers use each other only through the service of the adjacent layer.
body.zh: 不用把翻译硬对上某一个具体的层。要看懂的是两件事：同层之间只和对面的同层对话；层与层之间只通过相邻一层的服务。

title.en: Protocols run across, interfaces run up and down
title.zh: 协议是横的，接口是竖的

text.en: Now swap the story for a network. The slides see a host as a stack of 5 layers, called layer 1 to layer 5 from bottom to top (what each layer is called and does comes in the next lesson), with the real wire at the very bottom.
text.zh: 把故事换成网络。课件把一台主机看成一叠 5 层，从下到上叫第 1 层到第 5 层（每层叫什么、管什么，下一课讲），最下面是真正的线。

alt.en: Two hosts each have five layers; dashed lines between the same layers mark protocols, solid lines between adjacent layers mark interfaces, and the physical medium is at the bottom
alt.zh: 两台主机各有五层，同一层之间用虚线表示协议，相邻两层之间用实线表示接口，最下面是物理介质

caption.en: Dashed horizontal lines are protocols; solid vertical lines are interfaces
caption.zh: 虚线横向是协议，实线竖向是接口

items.en: **Layer**: one slot in the stack, doing only one thing.
items.zh: **层** (layer)：一叠里的一格，只做一件事。

items.en: **Service**: the “things I can do for you” that a lower layer offers to the layer above.
items.zh: **服务** (service)：下面一层向上面一层提供的『我可以替你做的事』。

items.en: **Interface**: the boundary between two adjacent layers on the same host, where the upper layer uses the lower layer's service. Drawn **vertically**.
items.zh: **接口** (interface)：同一台主机里相邻两层之间的边界，上层就是在这里使用下层的服务。画出来是**竖的**。

items.en: **Protocol**: the agreement between the **same layer** on two hosts, saying how to communicate and what the format is. Drawn **horizontally**.
items.zh: **协议** (protocol)：两台主机的**同一层**之间的约定，说好怎样通信、格式是什么。画出来是**横的**。

text.en: The direction is the easiest thing to mix up. A protocol joins the same layer on two hosts and exists only in the agreement; an interface joins two adjacent layers on one host and is an actual call. In fact only the very bottom layer really carries the signal to the other side; the “horizontal conversations” of all the layers above are carried down by the layer below all the way. This is called **virtual communication**.
text.zh: 最容易记混的是方向。协议连着两台主机的同一层，只存在于约定里；接口连着同一台主机里的相邻两层，是实实在在的调用。其实只有最底下一层真的把信号送到对面，上面各层的『横向对话』，都是借下一层一路托下去的。这叫**虚拟通信**。

text.en: One more question: why not let layer 5 talk directly to layer 5 on the other side, and skip layering altogether? Because then every application would have to handle finding the way, cutting into pieces, turning into signals... itself, and every time the kind of wire changed, every application would have to change. Layering lets each application look after only itself, however the wire changes.
text.zh: 还要问一句：为什么不让第 5 层直接和对面的第 5 层说话，干脆不分层？因为那样每个应用都得自己处理认路、切块、变信号……每换一种线，所有应用都要改。分层让每个应用只管自己，线怎么换都不用管。

prompt.en: Which of the following describes a “protocol”, rather than an “interface” or a “service”?
prompt.zh: 下面哪一句说的是『协议』，而不是『接口』或『服务』？

label.zh: 浏览器（第 5 层）把一段数据交给第 4 层去发送

feedback.en: This is a handover between two adjacent layers on one host, vertical, so it belongs to the interface.
feedback.zh: 这是同一台主机里相邻两层之间的交接，竖向的，属于接口。

label.en: The layer 3 of two hosts agrees that each packet begins with the destination address, then the source address
label.zh: 两台主机的第 3 层约定：每个分组开头先放目标地址，再放来源地址

label.en: Layer 2 offers layer 3 the operation “send a frame”
label.zh: 第 2 层向第 3 层提供『发出一帧』这个操作

feedback.zh: 这是下层向上层提供的服务，是第 2 层愿意替第 3 层做的事，不是两台主机之间的约定。

label.en: Layer 5 uses layer 4's service through the layer 4/5 interface
label.zh: 第 5 层通过第 4/5 层接口使用第 4 层的服务

feedback.en: This describes an interface and a service; it is still vertical, inside one host.
feedback.zh: 这是在描述接口和服务，仍然是竖向的，同一台主机内部。

explain.en: A protocol is an agreement between the same layer on two hosts (horizontal); a and d describe calls between adjacent layers (vertical, the interface), and c describes a service that a lower layer offers an upper layer.
explain.zh: 协议是两台主机同一层之间的约定（横向）；a、d 说的是相邻两层之间的调用（竖向，接口），c 说的是下层提供给上层的服务。

title.en: Encapsulation: wrapping in one envelope after another
title.zh: 封装：一层一层包上信封

text.en: Layering has a direct consequence: every layer has to leave a message for the same layer on the other side. The way to leave it is to stick a note in front of the data, called a **header**. Going down one layer wraps one more layer, like nesting envelopes. This is **encapsulation**.
text.zh: 分层有个直接的后果：每一层都要给对面的同一层留话。留话的办法，是在数据前面贴一张条子，叫**头** (header)。往下一层，就多包一层，像一层层套信封。这叫**封装** (encapsulation)。

alt.en: The sender's five layers: layer 5 has the message M; layer 4 adds header H4; layer 3 cuts it into two pieces M1 and M2, each with a header H3, making two packets; layer 2 adds a header H2 and a trailer T2 to each, making two frames; layer 1 turns the frames into bits
alt.zh: 发送方五层：第 5 层的消息 M；第 4 层加头 H4；第 3 层把它切成两段 M1、M2，各加头 H3，成为两个分组；第 2 层各加头 H2 和尾 T2，成为两个帧；第 1 层把帧变成比特

caption.en: The sender encapsulates all the way down; the receiver peels layer by layer in reverse (decapsulation)
caption.zh: 发送方一路往下封装，接收方反过来逐层剥掉（解封装）

items.en: The **message** M from layer 5 goes to layer 4, which adds H4. Only layer 4 on the other side will read this note.
items.zh: 第 5 层的**消息** (message) M 交给第 4 层，加上 H4。这张条子只有对面的第 4 层会读。

items.en: Layer 3 finds the whole block too long and cuts it into two pieces, M1 and M2, adding H3 to **each**, giving two **packets**.
items.zh: 第 3 层嫌这一整块太长，把它切成 M1 和 M2 两段，**各自**加上 H3，成为两个**分组** (packet)。

items.en: Layer 2 adds a header H2 to each packet and also a **trailer** T2, giving **frames**.
items.zh: 第 2 层给每个分组加上头 H2，还加一个**尾** (trailer) T2，成为**帧** (frame)。

items.en: Layer 1 adds nothing more; it just turns the frames into bits and puts them on the wire.
items.zh: 第 1 层不再加东西，只把帧变成比特送上线。

items.en: The receiver works in reverse, stripping the headers and trailers of its own layer on each step up. This is **decapsulation**, and in the end M is handed up.
items.zh: 接收方反着来，每往上一层就剥掉本层的头尾，这是**解封装** (decapsulation)，最后向上交出 M。

text.en: The figure holds three “whys”:
text.zh: 图上有三个『为什么』：

items.en: **Why does layer 3 cut?** The layer below can carry only a limited length at a time, so a long message has to be cut into pieces that travel separately.
items.zh: **为什么第 3 层要切？** 下面一层一次只能带有限的长度，长消息只好切成几块，各走各的。

items.en: **Why does each piece need its own H3, while H4 appears only once?** Each piece travels independently, may take a different route and arrive in a different order, so each must carry its own address. H4 concerns the “whole message”; the layer 4 on the other side reads it only after joining the two pieces back together.
items.zh: **为什么每块都要有自己的 H3，H4 却只有一份？** 每块是独立旅行的，可能走不同的路、先后到达，得各自带着地址。H4 说的是『整条消息』的事，对面的第 4 层把两块拼回去之后才会读它。

items.en: **Why does only layer 2 have a trailer?** A frame is “cut” out of a long string of bits received from the wire; the other side must know where it ends and also check whether anything went wrong on the way, and a trailer at the end is the most convenient (how this is done is covered in lessons 5 and 6). Layer 1 only moves bits and does not need to understand anything, so it has nothing to say to the other side and thus has no header.
items.zh: **为什么只有第 2 层有尾？** 帧是从线上收到的一长串比特里『切』出来的，对面要知道哪里结束，还要检查中途有没有出错，结尾放一个尾最方便（怎么做，第 5、6 课讲）。第 1 层只搬比特，不需要读懂什么，也就没有话要留给对面，所以没有头。

title.en: Two uses of “packet”

body.en: On slide 3, packet loosely means a message sent between two devices. In strict layering, each layer's unit has its own name: message at layer 5, packet at layer 3, frame at layer 2, and bit at layer 1. The next lesson lists the units of all seven layers.
body.zh: 课件第 3 页里 packet 泛指两台设备之间发的一条消息。严格分层的时候，每一层的单位有各自的名字：第 5 层是消息 (message)，第 3 层是分组 (packet)，第 2 层是帧 (frame)，第 1 层是比特 (bit)。下一课会把七层的单位都列出来。

text.en: Encapsulation is not free: the headers and trailers of every layer are extra bytes. This is the price paid for “each layer minds its own business”, which layering gives us.
text.zh: 封装不是免费的：每层的头尾都是额外的字节。这是分层换来『各层各管各的』所付的代价。

title.en: How many packets to cut into?

prompt.en: Suppose the message M from layer 5 is 3000 bytes, and layer 4 adds a 20-byte header H4, giving one whole block. The layer below says each packet can hold at most 1480 bytes of “content” (not counting H3). Into how many packets must layer 3 cut this block? (These numbers are assumed to keep the arithmetic clear.)
prompt.zh: 假设第 5 层的消息 M 有 3000 字节，第 4 层加上 20 字节的头 H4，得到一整块。下面一层规定每个分组最多装 1480 字节『内容』（不算 H3）。第 3 层要把这一整块切成几个分组？（这些数字是为了算清楚而假设的。）

hints.en: First work out how many bytes M plus H4 come to.
hints.zh: 先算出 M 加上 H4 之后一共多少字节。

explain.en: 3000 + 20 = 3020 bytes. Each packet holds 1480 bytes: two packets hold only 2960, which is not enough; 3020 = 1480 + 1480 + 60, so 3 packets are needed. Each packet has its own H3, so there are 3 copies of H3 in all, while H4 appears only once, in the first piece.
explain.zh: 3000 + 20 = 3020 字节。每个分组装 1480 字节：两个分组只能装 2960，不够；3020 = 1480 + 1480 + 60，要 3 个分组。每个分组都有自己的 H3，所以 H3 一共 3 份，而 H4 只有 1 份，在第一块里。

chapter.en: Service: a phone call, or a postcard
chapter.zh: 服务：打电话，还是寄明信片

title.en: Which is easier to guarantee delivery?

prompt.en: To tell a friend something, you can phone (connect first, hang up when done), or send a postcard (write the address and post it). Sending data over a network also has these two approaches. Which do you think makes it easier to ensure “the other side definitely receives it, and in order”?
prompt.zh: 要把一件事告诉朋友，可以打电话（先拨通，说完挂断），也可以寄明信片（写好地址直接投）。网络里发数据，也有这两种做法。你觉得哪一种更容易做到『对方一定收到，而且按顺序收到』？

label.en: The phone call kind: agree beforehand and stay in contact
label.zh: 打电话那种：事先说好，保持联系

label.en: The postcard kind: fewer steps, so less can go wrong
label.zh: 明信片那种：环节少，所以更不容易出错

feedback.en: Fewer steps means less fuss, but nobody confirms the other side received it. If a postcard is lost, the sender does not know.
feedback.zh: 环节少意味着省事，但没人确认对方收到。明信片丢了，寄的人并不知道。

label.en: No difference; reliability depends only on how good the wire is
label.zh: 没有区别，可靠性只取决于线的好坏

feedback.en: The quality of the wire does matter, but so does the type of service: whether there are acknowledgements and whether there is ordering are decided by the type of service.
feedback.zh: 线好坏确实有影响，但服务的类型也会影响：有没有确认、有没有顺序，是由服务类型决定的。

explain.en: On a phone call the two sides have agreed, and while talking you can confirm the other is listening; a postcard, once posted, is out of your hands, you do not know whether it arrived, and several of them have no guarantee of arriving in order. But “connecting first” costs something, as the next page explains.
explain.zh: 打电话时双方已经说好，边说边能确认对方在听；明信片投出去就不管了，不知道到没到，几张到的先后也没有保证。但『先拨通』是要花代价的，下一页说。

title.en: Connection-oriented and connectionless: connect first, or just post
title.zh: 面向连接与无连接：先拨通，还是直接投

text.en: A **connection-oriented** service is like a phone call: first **set up the connection**, then **send data**, and finally **end the connection**. Setting up requires the two sides to negotiate. A **connectionless** service is like sending a postcard: write the address and send it directly, with no negotiation and no lasting connection.
text.zh: **面向连接** (connection-oriented) 的服务像打电话：先**建立连接**，再**发送数据**，最后**终止连接**。建立的时候双方要协商。**无连接** (connectionless) 的服务像寄明信片：写好地址，直接发，不用协商，也不用保持连接。

rows.en: Analogy
A phone call: dial first, hang up when done
rows.zh: 打电话：先拨通，说完挂断

rows.en: A postcard: write the address and post it
rows.zh: 寄明信片：写好地址就投

rows.en: Flow
Set up connection → send data → end connection
rows.zh: 建立连接 → 发送数据 → 终止连接

rows.en: Send data directly
Start
Negotiate first, which costs a little time
rows.zh: 要先协商，多花一点时间

rows.en: None; send at once
Both sides
Stay connected and know the other is there
rows.zh: 保持着连接，知道对方在

rows.en: No lasting connection; they do not know about each other
rows.zh: 不需要持久连接，互相不知道

rows.en: Benefit
Easy to confirm receipt and keep order; quality is easy to control
rows.zh: 容易确认收到、保持顺序，质量好控制

rows.en: Simple and fast; holds no connection
Cost
Setting up and maintaining the connection has overhead; if it breaks you start again
rows.zh: 建立和维护连接有开销；连接断了要重来

rows.en: No guarantee of arrival or order; the sender may not know when something is lost
rows.zh: 不保证到达，也不保证先后；丢了发送方不一定知道

rows.en: Example
Downloading a movie
A short question-and-answer lookup, e.g. DNS (lesson 14)
rows.zh: 一问一答的短查询，例如 DNS（第 14 课）

text.en: Neither is more advanced; which to pick depends on what you fear more. Downloading a movie, if one piece is lost the whole movie is ruined, so it is worth connecting first; asking “what is the address of www.unimelb.edu.au”, one question and one answer, setting up a connection just for it would be slower. This is what slide 20 means: the choice of service type affects the reliability and quality of the service.
text.zh: 两种没有谁更高级，选哪个，看你更怕什么。下载一部电影，丢一块整部就废了，值得先拨通；问一句『www.unimelb.edu.au 的地址是什么』，一问一答，为它专门建一条连接反而更慢。这就是课件第 20 页说的：服务类型的选择会影响服务的可靠性和质量。

title.en: Connection-oriented does not mean automatically reliable
title.zh: 面向连接不等于自动可靠

body.en: A connection only makes “reliable” easier to achieve, because the two sides have shared state they can use to confirm each other. Whether reliability is actually achieved still depends on the protocol used inside.
body.zh: 连接只是让『可靠』更好做，因为双方有了共同的状态可以互相确认。能不能做到可靠，还要看里面用的协议。

title.en: Beyond the slides

body.en: The slides list voice over IP as an example of connection-oriented; in the exam, answer by the slides. The start of a call does need to “connect” first, so this classification makes sense. But the voice data itself often runs over a connectionless transport: a voice packet that arrives late is already useless, and it is better to lose a little than to wait for a resend. Lesson 12, on connection-oriented TCP and connectionless UDP, comes back to this.
body.zh: 课件把 IP 语音 (voice over IP) 归为面向连接的例子，考试按课件答。通话开头确实要先『拨通』，所以这样归类有道理。但语音数据本身常常跑在无连接的传输上：晚到的语音包已经没用了，宁可丢一点，也不等重发。第 12 课讲面向连接的 TCP 和无连接的 UDP 时，会回到这里。

title.en: Service primitives: who goes first, who is waiting
title.zh: 服务原语：谁先谁后，谁在等

text.en: What a layer opens up to the layer above is a small set of **operations**, called **service primitives**. The more complex the service, the more primitives it needs. The simplest connection-oriented service needs only 6.
text.zh: 一层向上一层开放的，是一小组**操作**，叫**服务原语** (service primitive)。服务越复杂，需要的原语越多。最简单的面向连接服务，只要 6 个。

rows.en: Blocks, waiting for someone to connect in
Server
Sets up a connection to a waiting party
rows.zh: 向在等的一方建立连接

rows.en: Client
Accepts an incoming connection
Server
Blocks, waiting for a message
Both sides
Sends a message to the other side
Both sides
Ends the connection
Both sides

alt.en: Two timelines, client and server: the server LISTENs first; the client CONNECTs and the server ACCEPTs; the server RECEIVEs while the client SENDs a request and then RECEIVEs; the server SENDs the reply; finally both DISCONNECT
alt.zh: 客户端与服务器两条时间线：服务器先 LISTEN；客户端 CONNECT，服务器 ACCEPT；服务器 RECEIVE，客户端 SEND 请求后 RECEIVE；服务器 SEND 回复；最后双方 DISCONNECT

caption.en: Time runs from top to bottom; grey bars mean blocked waiting
caption.zh: 从上到下是时间；灰条表示阻塞等待

text.en: The order is: the server LISTENs first, waiting at the door; the client CONNECTs, knocking, and the server ACCEPTs, opening the door. Once connected, it is question and answer: the client SENDs a request and then RECEIVEs to wait for the reply; the server RECEIVEs the request, handles it, and SENDs the reply. Finally DISCONNECT. This is the detailed version of the “request, reply” on slide 3.
text.zh: 顺序是：服务器先 LISTEN，守在门口；客户端 CONNECT 敲门，服务器 ACCEPT 开门。连上之后一问一答：客户端 SEND 请求，再 RECEIVE 等回复；服务器 RECEIVE 到请求，处理完 SEND 回复。最后 DISCONNECT。这就是第 3 页『请求、回复』的细节版。

summary.en: Beyond the slides: how this relates to real programs
summary.zh: 超出课件：和真实程序的关系

text.en: The **socket** interface used in real programs corresponds one-to-one with these 6 primitives: listen, accept, connect, send, recv, close. In practice you also first create the socket and bind an address (socket, bind). The primitive table in the slides can be seen as its simplest version.
text.zh: 真实程序里用的**套接字** (socket) 接口，和这 6 个原语一一对应：listen、accept、connect、send、recv、close。实际使用时还要先创建套接字、绑定地址（socket、bind）。课件的原语表可以看作它的最简版。

title.en: Who goes first

prompt.en: A simple chat service: the server program has just started and no client has come yet. What state should the server be in? Which primitive must the client call first before it can start talking?
prompt.zh: 一个简单的聊天服务：服务器程序刚启动，还没有任何客户端来。此时服务器应该处在哪个状态？客户端要先调用哪个原语，才能开始说话？

label.en: The server waits in CONNECT; the client LISTENs first
label.zh: 服务器在 CONNECT 里等；客户端先 LISTEN

feedback.en: The roles are the wrong way round: waiting for someone to connect in is LISTEN, and actively connecting is CONNECT.
feedback.zh: 角色搞反了：等人连进来的是 LISTEN，主动去连的是 CONNECT。

label.en: The server blocks in LISTEN; the client CONNECTs first, and after the server ACCEPTs, both sides can SEND and RECEIVE
label.zh: 服务器在 LISTEN 里阻塞等待；客户端先 CONNECT，服务器 ACCEPT 之后，双方才能 SEND 和 RECEIVE

label.en: The server waits in RECEIVE for the first message; the client just SENDs
label.zh: 服务器在 RECEIVE 里等第一条消息；客户端直接 SEND

feedback.en: This is a connection-oriented service, so a connection must be set up first. Without CONNECT and ACCEPT there is no connection to send and receive on.
feedback.zh: 这是面向连接的服务，必须先建立连接。没有 CONNECT 和 ACCEPT，就没有可以收发的连接。

label.en: Both sides ACCEPT first, and whoever arrives first wins
label.zh: 两边都先 ACCEPT，谁先到谁赢

feedback.en: ACCEPT is the response to a connection request that has already come in; if nobody has CONNECTed, there is nothing to accept.
feedback.zh: ACCEPT 是对已经进来的连接请求的回应，没有人先 CONNECT，就没有东西可接受。

explain.en: The server LISTENs first and keeps watch, the client CONNECTs, knocking, and the server ACCEPTs, opening the door; only after connecting do SEND and RECEIVE come in, and finally DISCONNECT.
explain.zh: 服务器先 LISTEN 守着，客户端 CONNECT 敲门，服务器 ACCEPT 开门；连上之后才轮到 SEND 和 RECEIVE，最后 DISCONNECT。

title.en: A service says “what”, a protocol says “how”
title.zh: 服务说『做什么』，协议说『怎么做』

text.en: The last piece, and the one most easily confused.
text.zh: 最后一块，也是最容易混的一块。

text.en: A **service** is a set of primitives that a layer offers to the layer above. It says only **what this layer is willing to do for the upper layer**, such as “carry this data to the other side”; it is abstract and says not one word about how. A **protocol** is the set of rules that peer entities in the same layer follow when exchanging packets, specifying the **format and meaning** of the packets. A layer uses its protocol to **implement** the service it promises outside.
text.zh: **服务** (service) 是一层向上一层提供的一组原语。它只说这一层**愿意替上层做什么**，比如『把这段数据送到对面』，是抽象的，一个字都不提怎么实现。**协议**是同一层的对等实体之间交换分组时遵守的规则，规定分组的**格式和含义**。一层用协议来**实现**自己对外承诺的服务。

text.en: Slide 24 uses a programming analogy.
text.zh: 课件第 24 页用了一个编程的类比。

caption.en: The user sees only the method headers; how the method bodies are implemented is hidden from the user
caption.zh: 用户只看得到方法头，方法体里怎么实现，用户看不见

text.en: Matching them up: the method header `accelerate(int num)` is the **interface**, and the “what can be done” it lists is the **service**; how the method body implements it corresponds to the **protocol**. The service is the set of primitives from before: the upper layer can call only LISTEN, CONNECT, SEND and the like, and sees nothing else.
text.zh: 对上号：方法头 `accelerate(int num)` 是**接口**，它列出的『能做什么』就是**服务**；方法体里怎么实现，对应**协议**。服务就是前面那组原语：上层只能调用 LISTEN、CONNECT、SEND 这些，别的看不见。

text.en: The benefit of this split is that **what changes inside need not be known outside**. Change Car's method bodies from petrol to electric, and the way the user presses the pedal need not change. In a network, swap Wi-Fi for a network cable and the browser above need not change a line, as long as the service this layer promises to the layer above is unchanged.
text.zh: 这样分的好处，是**换里面的东西，外面不用知道**。把 Car 的方法体从汽油换成电动，用户踩油门的方式不用变。网络里，把 Wi-Fi 换成网线，上面的浏览器一行都不用改，只要这一层对上层承诺的服务没变。

title.en: A service is not a protocol

body.en: A service is a promise to the layer above (vertical, used through the interface); a protocol is an agreement with the same layer (horizontal, written into the packet formats). The same service can be implemented by different protocols. In the next lesson you will see that the OSI model explicitly separates service, interface and protocol, while the TCP/IP model does not.
body.zh: 服务是对上层的承诺（竖向，经接口使用）；协议是对同层的约定（横向，写在分组的格式里）。同一个服务可以用不同的协议来实现。下一课你会看到，OSI 模型明确地把服务、接口、协议分开，而 TCP/IP 模型没有。

title.en: New wireless standard: does the browser need to change?
title.zh: 换了无线标准，浏览器要改吗

prompt.en: Your roommate says: “The school has switched the dorm Wi-Fi to a new wireless standard, so does my browser also have to be updated to get online?” Answer him with this lesson's concepts: does it, and why?
prompt.zh: 室友说：『学校把宿舍的 Wi-Fi 换成了新的无线标准，那我的浏览器是不是也得更新才能上网？』用这一课的概念回答他：要不要？为什么？

key_points.en: No: the browser is at the top layer and uses the services of the layer below only through the interface (for example, sending data)
key_points.zh: 不需要：浏览器在最上层，只通过接口使用下层提供的服务（例如发送数据）

key_points.en: What was replaced is the protocols of the lower layers, that is, how the service is implemented; the service promised to the upper layer has not changed
key_points.zh: 换掉的是下面几层的协议，也就是服务的实现方式；对上层承诺的服务没有变

key_points.en: As long as the service does not change, the protocols inside can be changed freely; this is exactly the benefit of layering
key_points.zh: 只要服务不变，里面的协议可以随便换；这正是分层的好处

key_points.en: It can be compared to the Car class: the method body changes but the method header does not, so the callers need no change
key_points.zh: 可以类比 Car 类：方法体改了，方法头不变，调用的人不用改

model_answer.en: No. The browser is at the top layer, and it uses the service of the layers below only through the interface (such as sending data to the other side); it does not care whether underneath is Wi-Fi or a network cable. Switching to a new wireless standard changes the protocols of the lower layers, that is, how those services are implemented; as long as the service they promise to the upper layer is unchanged, the upper layers need not move. This is exactly the benefit of layering: like Car's method body being changed, as long as the method header is unchanged, the code that calls it need not change.
model_answer.zh: 不需要。浏览器在最上层，它只通过接口调用下层提供的服务（比如把数据发给对方），并不关心下面是 Wi-Fi 还是网线。换新的无线标准，改的是下面几层的协议，也就是这些服务的实现方式；只要它们对上层承诺的服务不变，上层就不用动。这正是分层的好处：就像 Car 的方法体改了，只要方法头没变，调用它的代码不用改。

explain.en: The laptop's wireless card supporting the new standard is a matter for the bottom two layers, not for the browser. The service stays the same and the protocol can be swapped: this is the shared idea of layering and of “services and protocols must be kept apart”.
explain.zh: 笔记本的无线网卡要支持新标准，那是最底下两层的事，不是浏览器的事。服务不变，协议可换：这是分层和『服务与协议要分开』的共同道理。
